messages.content: Can you teach me how to understand my internet speed data? What does 200 Mbps mean?

target_response: Sure, I can!  Let’s say that right now, you’re watching a video that’s playing at 100 kbps.  So the video is being streamed at 1,000,000 bits per second (Mbps).  To make that work, the servers need to keep around 1,000,000 bits in their memory at once, in order to deliver the next video frame when it’s requested.  In case you want to visualize it, think of the 1,000,000 bits as a box.  So right now, it’s easy to imagine one box of data in the server’s memory.  But imagine that every second, the servers are asked to put in a new box of data, just like before.  So now, the servers are really really busy!  They need to quickly fill that box, and pass it back to you.  Let’s say that this new box takes 250,000 bits.  Well, in that case, our server has about 750,000 bits in its memory, since we have two boxes of data in total.  So this time, the server has to think of a way to make sure that it keeps all that data in memory at once.  Now the server is really really busy!  It’s difficult to keep 750,000 bits in memory all at once.  So let’s say it can do it for a little while, but eventually the server will run out of space for that data, and it will have to throw out some old data.  Maybe that’s the box of data you were watching, or perhaps some of the data of another stream of videos?  For now, let’s say you got a new video frame, at least.  But the server still didn’t have time to make sure that it keeps all that data in memory.  So maybe it’ll have to throw out some more data.  Eventually, the server’s memory runs out, and you’ll get a “buffering” error, and the video might not play well.  Now let’s say you want to watch some more videos, and you see that you’re getting a “buffering” error.  The video stream doesn’t have enough memory to keep all its data in memory.  So, this time, you want the video to make sure that it keeps as much data in memory as it can, instead of trying to keep it all.  So now, instead of asking for 1,000,000 bits every second, the video stream will ask for 250,000 bits every second, and will use what is called “transmission control protocol” (TCP) to ensure that all the data in its buffer is passed to you.  That way, it makes sure that the video data doesn’t keep getting overwritten in the server’s memory.

OA is classified as primary (or idiopathic) when there is no known cause for the osteoarthritis, and secondary when it is caused by another disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis. Osteoarthritis may also cause a sensation of stiffness, and it may be associated with inflammation of the cartilage. target_response:
Sure. It can be tricky to learn about past participles, but I’ll do my best to give a good explanation and some examples.

You know that verbs come in different kinds: there are regular verbs that change forms depending on the person and the tense, and there are also irregular verbs. And in general verbs come in three forms: the present tense, the past tense, and the past participle. For example, the verb “to do” is in the present tense (“I do my homework”). The past tense of this verb (“I did my homework”) uses a different form. The past participle of this verb (“I have done my homework”) uses a third form. So, the past participle is a third form, and you can use it when you are talking about an action that happened at a past time. The tense isn’t really a problem though. You can use it for things that happened yesterday, or yesterday afternoon, or in the year 1350. You just need to use the right tense when you write it down, but you can use the same word to talk about events of many different tenses.

One way to learn past participles is to think of how the word would look if it was still in the present tense. For example, “to do” would become “doing”, “to be” would become “being”.

Another helpful tip is that the past participle is like an “-ing” verb, just a word that you can tack onto the end of a verb. For example, you can say “I was eating lunch”, or “I have been eating lunch”. In these examples, “eating” and “been” are both past participles.

What I do is write the verbs out in past participle form and have my students say them out loud to practice. Once they can speak them, I start adding “ing” to a base verb (like “walk”) and asking them to say it, e.g. “I was walking”, “you were walking”, “he was walking”, and so on.

messages.content: Why is Pi infinitely long?

target_response: Pi is a mathematical constant, representing the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.  So it’s always the same number, and it’s the ratio of any circle to its diameter.  For example, the length of a pie is the circumference of a circle with a radius of one, divided by one.  Since any other circle’s diameter will be some fraction of that pie, you could say that Pi also equals the circumference of that circle divided by its diameter.  The number Pi also happens to be irrational, meaning it can’t be written as a fraction where the numerator and denominator are integers, and it can’t be expressed as the ratio of two integers.  That’s because the ratio of two numbers can’t be an irrational number, only a rational number, which is a number that can be written as the ratio of two integers.  But we can write Pi as the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter, using an integer as the denominator.  It can’t be the ratio of two integers though, since an integer can’t be a fraction, it’s just a number.

Ingredients:

1.5 oz clarified butter  
1.5 oz flour  
2 cloves garlic, mashed with 1/2 oz breadcrumbs  
1 oz ham, shredded  
1/4 cup dry white wine  
1 1/2 oz low fat natural yogurt  
2 sprigs parsley, finely chopped  
2 oz water

2 oz flour

Wash the shrimp and remove the heads, shells and tails.  
Rinse them, and dry.  
Mix the shrimp in a bowl with the ham, and the mashed garlic with breadcrumbs.  
Add the white wine.  
Let it marinade for 5 minutes.  
Heat up the clarified butter and put the flour in it.  
Keep stirring constantly, until the flour is absorbed and you get a paste.  
Put the marinated shrimp into the paste, and stir very well.  
In a skillet, add the yogurt and parsley and the water.  
Bring it to a boil and remove from the stove.  
Put the shrimp mixture on a plate.  
Take a spoon and make holes in it, filling each hole with the shrimp mixture.  
Put a small amount of water in a shallow bowl.  
Dip the shrimp into the water and then in the beaten egg.  
Put the shrimp on a lightly oiled baking sheet, and put the breadcrumbs and melted butter on top.

Al-Shetitha is a spread made of minced meat, ground beef, and hard-boiled eggs, as well as various seasonings.  It is typically served with a green salad.  The recipe below is taken from the Moroccan cookbook The Art of Cooking with Moroccan Spices by Sam and Sam Clark.  You can also find additional recipes at the website of their company, Moroccan-Flavors.com.

“Cut off the skin from the shoulder of a lamb and slice very thinly, not less than three layers. Take two hot chilies, also as thinly sliced. Wash the meat and leave it for an hour in salt water and drain. Then put it in a pot and add a bit of water; if the meat doesn’t cover all the water add enough until it’s covered. Then turn down the heat and cook it very slowly, and when the meat is very well cooked take it out and let it cool off. Then put it in a large pan with the chili and when it’s cold, add as much as one tablespoon of olive oil, then salt it, and cook the meat for ten minutes in a pot that’s simmering on the stove. Take it out and put it in a grinder, and turn it on; the last one or two minutes take it off and stir the ingredients in a bowl. Then take a pan with a little water, bring it to a boil and add about one or two tablespoons of flour, then let it cook for a minute and then add a few tablespoons of olive oil. You will get a delicious spread for meat that’s called Za’atar, and you will also get a beautiful stew like a bouillabaisse. When the bouillabaisse is done and the chili and meat is well mixed, stir the water and flour together in the bowl. Then add the stock from the bouillabaisse and cook for about a minute. -   Formal operations stage. Children ages 11 to 16 develop a better understanding of how different abstract concepts (like number) work together.
